sentence: A band neutrophil has an unsegmented, elongated, narrow band shape of uniform thickness with a single lobe, whereas a segmented neutrophil has a nucleus with 2 to 5 lobes joined by thin filaments [2][3].
The cytoplasm of both cell types is pink or nearly colorless with moderate granules, but the key difference is the nuclear morphology.
Segmented neutrophils display multiple lobes, while bands have a single, unsegmented nucleus [3].

Toxic changes in neutrophils on a film include toxic granulation, which appears as dark blue-black peroxidase-positive granules in the cytoplasm, toxic vacuolation seen as clear, circular unstained areas, and Dohle bodies, which are pale blue, round or elongated inclusions containing remnant RNA near the cell periphery [1].
These features are typically observed in mature neutrophils and bands, often alongside a left shift with increased immature granulocytes [1].

A hypersegmented neutrophil has two or more lobes in the nucleus, with at least one neutrophil showing 6 or more nuclear segments or at least 5% of circulating neutrophils with 5 nuclear segments [1].

Hypersegmentation is considered a maturation 'accident' resulting from aberrant endomitosis during neutrophil development, and it may be associated with conditions such as megaloblastic anemia, iron deficiency anemia, or renal failure [1][2].
It can also be seen in some scenarios like infections or tumor responses, suggesting it may mark a particular functional state rather than just maturation [2].

Smudge cells are often a result of fragile leukocytes, such as lymphocytes or neutrophils, rupturing during smear preparation, which creates artifacts that appear as naked nuclei or cell fragments [1][2].
In conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), numerous small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells are common due to the fragility of these cells [4].
Additionally, NET formation by neutrophils can produce NET-like smudge cells that are not artifacts but reflect neutrophil activation and cell death processes [2][3][5].

Reactive lymphocytosis is caused by various infectious and noninfectious stimuli, including viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, measles, mumps, varicella, influenza, hepatitis A/B/C, and rubella, as well as certain bacterial infections like Bordetella pertussis, Bartonella henselae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Brucella, and Treponema pallidum [1].

Noninfectious causes include autoimmune diseases, medications (e.g., carbamazepine, vancomycin, allopurinol), and stress reactions such as trauma, acute cardiac ischemia, vigorous exercise, and smoking [1].
Persistent basophilia, defined as lasting more than 8 months, is always suggestive of a neoplastic hematologic disorder [2].

A left shift indicates an increase in circulating immature neutrophil precursors, such as bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts, often associated with conditions like infection, inflammation, or stress [1][2].
It is usually seen on the peripheral blood smear when toxicity is present and may be accompanied by toxic changes like granulation, vacuolation, or dohle bodies in neutrophils [1][5].
A severe neutrophilia with a left shift is termed a leukaemoid reaction [2][3].
Monocytosis occurs in acute and chronic inflammatory conditions, including atherosclerosis and infections, as it results from systemic inflammation that recruits monocytes to inflammatory sites [4].
It can also be associated with reactive causes such as infections that produce myelomonocytosis, mimicking leukemia [3].
A segmented neutrophil typically has two to five lobes connected by a filament [1].
Cytoplasmic vacuoles in neutrophils are indicative of phagocytosis or autophagocytosis, often associated with bacterial or yeast ingestion in septic conditions [3].
Their presence can be more prominent in cases of bacteremia or severe infection, reflecting the neutrophil's active response to invading pathogens [2][3].
Many cell abnormalities can result from storage-induced cytological lesions, which are influenced by factors such as time and temperature between blood collection and film preparation [1].
These lesions may cause nuclear and cytoplasmic anomalies that can mimic or obscure true cell morphology, leading to potential misinterpretation.
Variability in laboratory methods, including fixation and staining protocols, further contributes to the likelihood of artifacts appearing on blood films [1].

Interleukin-3 (IL-3) is the most potent growth factor for basophil differentiation and maturation, promoting their development from progenitor cells and supporting their viability and activation [1][2].
Other regulators include granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), IL-5, transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) [1][2].
These cytokines and growth factors contribute to increased basophil production and activity in various conditions.
A band neutrophil has an unsegmented nucleus and is considered a less mature form of neutrophil, often seen in a left shift during infection or inflammation [1].
The presence of immature neutrophils, such as bands, can indicate an increased demand for neutrophils, typically in response to bacterial infections or other inflammatory conditions [1].
Toxic changes like toxic granulation, vacuolation, and Dohle bodies are also associated with immature or activated neutrophils, reflecting a response to infection or toxicity [4].
Therefore, the maturity status of neutrophils can be relevant in interpreting the clinical significance of the findings.
Monocytosis, or elevated monocyte counts, commonly occurs in acute and chronic inflammatory conditions, including atherosclerosis [3].
Inflammation and dyslipidaemia are key factors that promote the accumulation of classical CD14 ++ CD16 − monocytes in plaques, leading to pro-inflammatory macrophages [5].

Additionally, hypercholesterolaemia is associated with increased levels of circulating monocytes, and lipid-lowering treatments can decrease these counts, indicating a link between high cholesterol and monocytosis [3].

Eosinophilia can be caused by primary mechanisms involving clonal expansion of eosinophils due to somatic mutations, or secondary mechanisms as a response to exogenous cytokines from conditions such as infections, allergic diseases, connective tissue disorders, vasculitis, malignancies, or endocrinopathies [1][2].
Hematological disorders may involve intrinsic mechanisms, with eosinophils derived from malignant clones, or extrinsic mechanisms triggered by cytokines [3].
Medications are also a common cause, with drug reactions potentially leading to eosinophilia, including severe cases like DRESS [4].
Eosinophil production and recruitment are regulated by cytokines such as IL-5, IL-3, and GM-CSF, which influence their differentiation, maturation, and tissue infiltration [5].

Parasites such as Trichinella spiralis, Fasciola hepatica, Schistosoma species, Echinococcus, Strongyloides stercoralis, Ancylostoma duodenale, and Opisthorchis are associated with high eosinophil counts, often exceeding 1 × 10^9/L [2][4].
These helminth infections can lead to acute eosinophilia with symptoms like fever, myalgia, and abdominal pain, and are common causes of eosinophilia in endemic areas [4].

A drug reaction can cause eosinophilia, which may be associated with tissue infiltration and organ involvement, including systemic symptoms such as fever and rash, particularly in severe cases like DRESS [1].
However, eosinophilia is neither sensitive nor specific for drug reactions, and blood eosinophil levels may be absent even when tissue eosinophils are present [1].
Recognizing the clinical context and associated symptoms is important for diagnosis and management.
Eosinophil counts exceeding 0.5 × 10^9/L are considered eosinophilia, with hypereosinophilia defined as counts ≥1.5 × 10^9/L [4][5].
Mild eosinophilia ranges from 0.5 to 1.49 × 10^9/L, moderate from 1.5 to 5.0 × 10^9/L, and severe above 5.0 × 10^9/L [4][5].

The significance of the count depends on the presence of organ damage and clinical context, with counts ≥1.5 × 10^9/L being particularly relevant for hypereosinophilia and hypereosinophilic syndromes [1][3][5].

Eosinophil granules contain a crystalline core composed of major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil peroxidase (EPO), eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN), and eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), surrounded by a matrix that includes these proteins and other mediators such as cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, and enzymes [1][2][4].
Small granules contain acid phosphatase and arylsulfatase, while secretory vesicles or microgranules hold receptors, adhesion molecules, and albumin [1].
Lipid bodies, which differ from granules, are sites of leukotriene synthesis [1].
Eosinophils and basophils are increased in response to inflammatory processes, particularly in conditions like COPD, where tissue inflammation and immune responses are involved [5].
The accumulation of these cells is associated with a type 2 immune microenvironment, indicated by increased GATA3 expression, which promotes eosinophil and basophil recruitment and activation [5].
Such increases are often linked to disease progression and tissue remodeling in advanced stages of COPD [5].
Neutropenia is most commonly caused by viral infections, medications such as azathioprine and cyclophosphamide, and hypersplenism [2].
Autoimmune mechanisms, including the generation of autoantibodies against neutrophils, and functional defects involving immune complexes or drug effects, can also contribute [2].
A leukemoid reaction typically shows a white blood cell count less than 12×10^9/L, with a predominance of mature neutrophils and no significant basophilia or myeloid immaturity in the blood [1].

In contrast, CML is characterized by a neutrophilic proliferation often associated with basophilia, increased myeloid precursors, and the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR::ABL1 fusion gene [5].
Cytogenetic or molecular studies are essential for definitive differentiation, especially when blood counts are ambiguous [5].
A Pelger-Huet cell is a neutrophil with a hyposegmented nucleus, often appearing as a single round (unilobed) or dumbbell-shaped (bilobed) nucleus [1][2].
It is associated with the Pelger-Huet anomaly, a benign condition where granulocytes show normal granulation and mature chromatin, with 50-90% of neutrophils affected in congenital cases [1].
The anomaly results from a mutation in the Lamin β-receptor gene and does not impair cell function [1].
A Dohle body is a pale blue, round or elongated cytoplasmic inclusion containing remnant ribosomal RNA in parallel rows, often present in mature neutrophils and bands near the cell periphery [3][5].
They are non-specific and can appear in various conditions such as infections, pregnancy, cancer, and burns [3].
Dohle bodies are associated with toxic changes in neutrophils, which may include toxic granulation and vacuolation [3].

Primary granules contain enzymes such as MPO, serine proteases (including neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G), and antimicrobial peptides, and are present from the promyelocyte stage of neutrophil development [1][2].
Secondary granules contain enzymes like collagenase (MMP-1), lysozyme, lactoferrin, and NADPH oxidase, and appear in the myelocyte/metamyelocyte stage [2].

The main difference is that primary granules are involved in initial antimicrobial activity and tissue remodeling, while secondary granules contain enzymes and proteins that support microbial killing and immune responses during later stages of neutrophil maturation [1][2].
The available sources do not specify an exact number of bands that are considered too many.
However, they note that normally, band neutrophils should be less than 8% of circulating neutrophils [4].

A large lymphocyte typically has a nucleus that may be indented or folded, with a nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio of approximately 2:1 to 5:1, and may contain nucleoli, with pale blue cytoplasm that can be granular or agranular [2].

A monocyte, on the other hand, is usually larger with abundant, often basophilic cytoplasm that may contain vacuoles, and has a nucleus that is often kidney-shaped or folded, with less condensed chromatin [3].
Morphologically, monocytes are distinguished by their larger size and more irregular nuclear shape compared to small lymphocytes.

Reactive lymphocytes, such as atypical lymphocytes in COVID-19, often display heterogeneous morphologies, including large lymphocytes with pale or blue cytoplasm, lymphoplasmacytoid cells, and Downey types I, II, and III, with features like irregular nuclear contours and prominent nucleoli [1][5].
In contrast, neoplastic lymphocytes tend to be monomorphous and may require additional studies like flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or molecular testing for definitive diagnosis [3][5].
Recognizing the heterogeneity and associated morphological features, along with serial blood evaluations and subset analysis, can aid in distinguishing reactive from neoplastic processes [1][5].

An atypical lymphocyte is a type of reactive lymphocyte, often associated with infectious or immune responses, and may exhibit heterogeneous morphology, including features like lymphoplasmacytic or pleomorphic appearance [1][2][3].

The terminology can vary, with some sources distinguishing "abnormal" or "atypical" lymphocytes as suspect reactive or neoplastic, but generally, atypical lymphocytes are considered reactive in the context of infections like COVID-19 [1][3][4].
A monocyte nucleus can have variable shapes, including folds and kidney-shaped forms, with loose, lacy, violet chromatin [1].
It may contain nucleoli and exhibit nuclear segmentations, especially in immature or abnormal monocytes [3].

A monocytosis indicates CMML when it is persistent, with monocyte counts of ≥ 0.5 × 10^9/L (≥ 10% of WBC), lasts for more than 4 months, and is associated with clonality confirmed by somatic mutations or chromosomal aberrations [1][3].
Flow cytometry showing an increased proportion of classical monocytes (CD14+/CD16−) ≥ 94% can also support the diagnosis [4].
Basophil granules are metachromatic, staining pink or red with toluidine blue due to their high proteoglycan content [1].
They are typically large and dense, and their metachromatic staining indicates the presence of proteoglycans in the granules [1].
Specific stains like chloroacetate esterase react with mastocytic granules but not with basophilic granules, which can aid in differentiation [2].
Yes, basophils can increase in response to reactive (non-clonal) causes, with persistent basophilia (>8 months) suggesting a neoplastic hematologic disorder [4].

A slide requires manual review when the blood film quality or stain quality is inadequate for accurate cell identification, or when morphological abnormalities are detected that may impact diagnosis, such as in cases of suspected hematological pathology or abnormal differential counts [3][4].
Manual review is also critical in situations like acute promyelocytic leukemia, where prompt diagnosis is essential [4].
Additionally, manual review may be necessary if automated slide makers cause traumatic morphological changes or artifacts that could mislead interpretation [1][3].
Prolonged storage of blood samples in EDTA can lead to a significant decrease in segmented neutrophils over time, especially after 24 hours, which may affect differential counts [1][5].
The morphology of leukocytes remains sufficiently preserved within 4 to 8 hours for reliable assessment, but extended delays may compromise cell integrity and counts [2].

Additionally, neutrophil nuclear morphology, such as hyper-segmentation, may be influenced by functional states or maturation processes, but the sources do not specify effects of time on nuclear shape [3][4].
An absolute eosinophil count (AEC) measures the actual number of eosinophils in peripheral blood, expressed as cells per unit volume (e.g., 0.5–1.49 × 10^9/L) [2][3].

A relative count refers to the percentage of eosinophils among total leukocytes, which can be affected by changes in other white blood cell populations and may not accurately reflect eosinophil levels alone [1].
The absolute count provides a direct quantification, whereas the relative count indicates proportion within the total white blood cell count.

A neutrophil is a polymorphonuclear leukocyte that plays a key role in innate immunity by neutralizing and killing pathogens such as bacteria, fungi, and protozoans through phagocytosis, degranulation, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production [2][3].
It can also form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which capture and eliminate microbes but often lead to neutrophil death [1][2][3][4].

Additionally, neutrophils migrate from the bloodstream to sites of infection or inflammation via a multistep process involving adhesion, crawling, and transmigration, contributing to tissue remodeling and inflammatory responses [3][5].
A neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) is a web-like structure composed of decondensed nuclear chromatin and granular proteins such as neutrophil elastase, myeloperoxidase, and others [2][5].

NETs are formed as part of the innate immune response to trap, neutralize, and kill pathogens like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and they can also be involved in sterile inflammation and tissue damage [2][5].

They may be expelled through various mechanisms, including a form of cell death called NETosis, or independently of cell death, resulting in structures that function in antimicrobial defense and potentially contribute to pathological processes [4][5].
Neutrophil granules contain a variety of molecules with proteolytic, antimicrobial, cytotoxic, and oxidative activities.
Primary granules include myeloperoxidase (MPO), neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, and antimicrobial peptides like defensins [1][2].
Secondary granules contain lactoferrin, lysozyme, and NADPH oxidase, while tertiary granules harbor gelatinases (MMP-2 and MMP-9), cathepsin, and lipocalin 2 [2].
These granules are essential for neutrophil functions such as microbial killing and tissue remodeling [2].

An eosinophil is a polymorphonuclear cell derived from hematopoietic precursors that plays a crucial role in defense against parasitic infections, releasing toxic granule proteins to combat parasites [1][5].
They are also involved in mediating inflammatory processes, tissue repair, and modulating immune responses, particularly in allergic diseases and eosinophilic disorders [3][5].
Eosinophils produce and store biologically active molecules, influencing homeostasis and tissue integrity, and can contribute to tissue damage in cases of persistent activation [3].
Eosinophils can be damaging to tissue because they release toxic granule proteins, cytokines, and mediators that induce inflammation, fibrosis, and thrombosis [1][3].
When they undergo persistent activation, their toxic content can cause tissue damage and organ dysfunction, especially in hypereosinophilic syndromes [1][3].
Their granules contain cationic proteins like major basic protein and eosinophil neurotoxin, which are highly toxic to parasites, bacteria, fungi, viruses, and host tissues [5].
Basophil granules contain proteoglycans that stain metachromatically with toluidine blue, indicating their large proteoglycan content [4].
These granules can release proinflammatory cytokines, histamine, and other mediators upon activation, contributing to immune modulation, allergic responses, and inflammation [3].
The granules' contents are involved in amplifying type 2 immune responses and mediating host defense, but their release can also promote pathogenic inflammation [3].

Basophil granules stain so dark because they contain a large amount of proteoglycans that take up metachromatic stains, such as toluidine blue or methylene blue, resulting in pink or red coloration [1].

A basophil is a circulating hematopoietic cell derived from multipotent stem cells, with metachromatic granules rich in histamine but lacking tryptase, and it expresses high-affinity IgE receptors (FcεRI) [5].

In contrast, mast cells are tissue-resident, contain tryptase in their granules, and have different characteristics depending on their location, such as responsiveness to opiates and substance P in the skin [2].
Markers like CD123 and CD11b indicate basophil differentiation, whereas tryptase and CD117 are associated with mast cells [1].
Lymphocytes participate in cell-mediated immunity when activated, involving specific surface markers such as CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8, and CD25 [4].
Neutrophils primarily neutralize pathogens through phagocytosis, release of reactive oxygen species, and formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) [1].
Therefore, lymphocytes have a specialized role in adaptive immunity that neutrophils do not perform.
A neutrophil's nucleus is segmented to enhance its deformability, which is critical for migration through mechanical barriers during immune responses [2][5].
The segmentation, such as hyposegmentation seen in Pelger-Huet anomaly, is associated with decreased nuclear deformability and impaired neutrophil migration [5].
This structural feature allows neutrophils to efficiently traverse tissues and reach sites of inflammation [2].
